case_title: Rakesh & Another v. State of Madhya Pradesh
accused_victim_relationship: Acquaintance (residents of the same village); alleged prior dispute over utensils that the victim refused to give, with alleged threats
statutory_provisions: IPC s.302; Arms Act s.25 (cited in FIR)
evidence_type: Eyewitness (PW11); medical (post-mortem by PW8); recovery of weapons on disclosure statements; investigating officer testimony; arrest
confession: No confession noted; disclosure statements leading to recovery of weapons were relied on
aggravating_circumstances: Heinous crime (court's description); multiple sharp-edged wounds to neck, chest and abdomen
trial_court_outcome: Convicted under s.302 IPC; rigorous imprisonment for life and fine of Rs. 2,000 each (default one year)
high_court_outcome: Appeals dismissed; conviction upheld (judgment dated 15.12.2006, after remand; earlier 10.2.2005 decision set aside by Supreme Court)
neutral_facts: On 5 March 1996, at about 11.30 a.m. on a market day, the victim was attacked in front of a house in a village by three men, including the accused, who were then caught on the spot by the victim's nephew, who had been following the victim and had raised an alarm. Several people gathered, but the assailants broke free and fled. The victim was taken to hospital, where a doctor declared him dead. A post-mortem examination was conducted the same afternoon by a doctor who found three incised wounds, on the neck, chest and abdomen, all caused by sharp-edged weapons. The doctor opined that death had occurred three to six hours before the examination; the doctor did not fix an exact time of death. The victim's nephew testified that he saw the accused, with another man, strike the victim with a knife, a gupti and a katarna, and that he had been at a short distance on a main road with an unobstructed view. He said that one of the accused had earlier wanted utensils from the victim, who refused, and had threatened him. Other persons present were questioned, and some did not support the prosecution. The nephew lodged a first information report at a police station about one kilometre away within about an hour, naming all three accused and describing the overt acts and the motive. The investigating officer was examined, the accused were arrested, and the weapons were recovered on the basis of the accused's disclosure statements. The accused and the victim were residents of the same village. The defence examined one witness who gave the time of the incident as 11.00 a.m.
physical_harm: Death; three incised wounds on the neck, chest and right abdomen caused by sharp-edged weapons
motive: alleged: accused wanted utensils from the deceased, who refused, and the accused threatened him
key_evidence_accepted: Testimony of the eyewitness nephew (PW11); post-mortem evidence (PW8); investigating officer's testimony (PW21); PW9's statement; arrests; weapon recoveries on disclosure statements; prompt FIR
witness_credibility: Eyewitness nephew (PW11) found trustworthy and natural despite being a related witness, scrutinised carefully; PW21 found natural with no animus; PW6 and PW12 did not fully support prosecution, but PW11 was relied on
custody_duration: Rakesh served more than 14 years and was prematurely released; Rajesh served about 7½ years and remained in jail
trial_duration: offence: 5.3.1996; trial judgment: 21.2.1997; High Court: 15.12.2006 (after remand; earlier decision dated 10.2.2005 set aside); Supreme Court: 19.9.2011 (judgment date)
legal_representation: Appellants: Siddharth Aggarwal, Aditya Wadhwa, Stuti Gujral, Senthil Jagadeesan. State: Vibha Datta Makhija
investigation_status: FIR registered; arrests made; weapons recovered; chargesheet filed; trial completed in Sessions court
procedural_irregularity: High Court's 10.2.2005 decision was rendered in absence of the appellants' counsel; Supreme Court set it aside and remanded
appeal_history: Trial court: convicted under s.302 IPC (21.2.1997). High Court: first decision 10.2.2005 set aside by Supreme Court (20.7.2006) and remanded; High Court dismissed on 15.12.2006. Supreme Court: appeal dismissed
prosecution_argument: No rule bars reliance on close relatives' evidence but it must be scrutinised; medical evidence on time of death is not conclusive; concurrent findings of fact should not be disturbed
defence_argument: Eyewitnesses PW10 and PW11 could not have been present; ocular evidence contradicts medical evidence on time of death; PW11 is closely related to the deceased and no independent witness supported his presence; mutually destructive evidence should be discarded
legal_principle_applied: Ocular evidence has primacy over medical evidence unless totally irreconcilable; related witness evidence is admissible if trustworthy but must be carefully scrutinised; exact time of death cannot be fixed; minor discrepancies do not discard evidence
precedent_relied_upon: State of U.P. v. Hari Chand (2009) 13 SCC 542; Abdul Sayeed v. State of MP (2010) 10 SCC 259; Bhajan Singh v. State of Haryana (2011) 7 SCC 421; Mangu Khan v. State of Rajasthan AIR 2005 SC 1912; Baso Prasad v. State of Bihar AIR 2007 SC 1019; Kartik Malhar v. State of Bihar (1996) 1 SCC 614; Himanshu @ Chintu v. State (NCT of Delhi) (2011) 2 SCC 36; Kishan Singh v. Gurpal Singh AIR 2010 SC 3624; Manju Ram Kalita v. State of Assam (2009) 13 SCC 330; Leela Ram v. State of Haryana (1999) 9 SCC 525
